grade.first_issue: The claim that \(C_jn^{k/d}+D_j\) cannot approach integers along an infinite subset unless \(k/d\) is integral is false; for example, \(\sqrt n\) is integral along the infinite subset of perfect squares.
grade.summary: The final classification is correct, and the conditional factorization argument after \(P(Q(x))=x^{2024}\) contains useful progress. However, the proof obtains that identity through invalid asymptotic inferences applying only on an arbitrary infinite subsequence. It also falsely concludes that a rational \(c\) satisfying \(c^d=1/a_d\) with \(a_d\in\mathbb Z\) must be integral. These are central gaps requiring a new argument.
strengths: Correctly states the answer and gives a valid verification that every listed polynomial has the required property.
Correctly observes, conditional on \(P(Q(x))=x^{2024}\), that \(P\) can have only one distinct complex root.

errors.description: An arbitrary infinite subsequence can make a nonintegral power arbitrarily close to integers, so the argument that \(d\mid2024\) is invalid.
From \(x_n-Q(n)\to0\) with \(x_n\in\mathbb Z\), it does not follow that \(x_n=Q(n)\) eventually; hence the decisive polynomial identity \(P(Q(x))=x^{2024}\) is unsupported.
The inference \(c\in\mathbb Q\) and \(c^d=1/a_d\Rightarrow c\in\mathbb Z\) is false; for instance, \(c=\tfrac12\), \(d=2\), and \(a_d=4\).
